units.title: Compiling, linking, loading, ABI and C linkage
outcomes: Trace a source file through preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking and loading, naming each artifact.
Diagnose a missing declaration, missing definition or missing shared library at the responsible stage.
Explain which ABI and ownership agreements a C-linkage boundary still needs.
units.why: A native extension can compile successfully yet fail to link or import. Separating these stages lets you repair the boundary rather than change unrelated source code.

next.note: Encode the pipeline as repeatable targets.
Apply compatibility and ownership contracts at import and call time.

study.title: Compilation Process
study.locator: Recap of the Pipeline; Stage 1 through Stage 4; Putting It Together: A Two-File Build; Mapping Errors to Stages
study.depth: Use the artifacts and error examples. Do not adopt the lesson's unmeasured optimization speedup ranges or its mention of trigraph translation: trigraphs were removed in C++17.

study.title: Language linkage
study.locator: Explanation and Notes, including the __cplusplus conditional header example

study.title: Cross-compiler interfaces
study.locator: I.26: If you want a cross-compiler ABI, use a C-style subset

study.title: Linux dynamic linker/loader
study.locator: DESCRIPTION, including dependency search order and Dynamic string tokens; ENVIRONMENT entry LD_DEBUG
study.depth: Stop before legacy hardware-capability directories and auditing.

focus: A declaration lets a translation unit type-check a call. A definition supplies the implementation; an object file can still contain unresolved symbols.
Use -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic and -g for development. Compare -O0 and -O2 artifacts without treating optimization as a correctness fix or a promised speedup.
ABI covers calling conventions, representation and binary compatibility. extern C linkage does not make STL objects, exceptions or allocators portable across arbitrary binaries.
The Linux loader searches for shared objects at runtime. A link-time -L directory is not automatically a runtime search path.
units.reproduce: With g++ 15.2, -std=c++20 -O0 -g on Linux x86-64, define extern "C" int inc(int x) { return x + 1; } in one translation unit and declare it in another whose main returns inc(41) == 42 ? 0 : 1. Produce preprocessed text with -E, assembly with -S and objects with -c. Inspect nm: the defining object has T inc and the caller U inc. Linking only the caller fails with undefined reference to inc; linking both objects succeeds and exits zero. Compare -O2 assembly, recording the flags rather than promising specific instructions.
traps: Including a header is not the same as linking the implementation that its declarations require.
An unmangled C symbol is not a complete stable ABI. Agree on widths, buffer lengths, ownership, error codes and compatible platform conventions.
Debug symbols and optimization are independent choices. Optimized code can have debug information while some source variables are optimized out.

selfTest.q: Why can -c succeed when a called function has no definition?
selfTest.a: The declaration suffices for compilation. The object records an unresolved symbol for the linker to resolve.

selfTest.q: An executable links but reports a missing .so when started. Which stage needs investigation?
selfTest.a: Loading. Inspect the dependency name and runtime search paths, not just the source include path.

selfTest.q: Does extern C make a function returning std::vector<int> safe for an arbitrary C caller?
selfTest.a: No. It changes language linkage, not the vector representation, C type system or allocator ownership contract.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: document the native component's build artifacts and ABI, and diagnose one missing-symbol or runtime-library failure.
units.stopWhen: You reproduce the two-object link and correctly classify a missing header, unresolved symbol and missing runtime library, with a written C-boundary ownership contract.

fit.note: Kept AlgoMaster and the pool's ABI references; added Linux ld.so because runtime loading and library discovery lacked a concrete locator.

units.title: Integer representation, pointers, references and spans
outcomes: Explain integer widths, signed and unsigned conversions, and the difference between representation and overflow rules.
Read pointer and reference code without losing the array bounds or the referent's lifetime.
Implement a span-based operation with explicit bounds and empty-input tests.
units.why: Native interfaces pass addresses and counts rather than Python objects. A correct value in the wrong integer type or a pointer without its extent can cross that boundary unsafely.

next.note: Turn element offsets into byte-address calculations.
Keep the storage behind each borrowed view alive.

study.title: Integer representation and data models
study.locator: Integral types: Standard integer types and Character types; Range of values; Data models
study.depth: Skip floating-point tables and C++26 reflection. Use the C++20 rules.

study.title: Integer promotions and conversions
study.locator: Integral promotion and Numeric conversions: Integral conversions

study.title: Pointer Arithmetic
study.locator: The Setup: What Pointer Arithmetic Means through The Rules: One Past the End and Undefined Behavior

study.title: References Basics
study.locator: What a Reference Is through References as Return Values; Common Mistakes
study.depth: Use the local-reference and dangling-return examples. The named-local rule of thumb is not the full set of temporary-lifetime extension rules.

study.title: std::span
study.locator: Opening contract; Member functions: Element access, Observers and Subviews; Notes and Example
study.depth: Use the C++20 interface. span::at is C++26, so write an explicit bounds check for this unit.

focus: C++20 requires two's-complement signed representation, but signed arithmetic overflow is still undefined. Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2 to the type's bit width.
Conversions and promotions happen before arithmetic and comparisons. Narrow unsigned operands can promote to int, so inspect the expression type, not only the declared variable type.
Pointer arithmetic advances by elements within an array, including its one-past position. That position may be compared but not dereferenced.
A reference aliases an object; assignment through it does not rebind it. A span carries a contiguous extent but neither owns storage nor checks operator[] in C++20.
units.reproduce: Using g++ 15.2 with -std=c++20 -O0 -g, write a function taking std::span<int> that doubles its elements. int a[]{2,4,6} becomes {4,8,12}; an empty span performs no writes. Write a separate checked accessor that throws std::out_of_range when i >= size(), and test i == 3 on that array. Predict and check that numeric_limits<unsigned>::max() + 1u is zero and that int n = -1 compared as n < 1u is false. Do not execute signed overflow to infer a wraparound rule: its behavior is undefined and no particular output is guaranteed.
traps: Replacing a pointer with a span does not extend the underlying array's lifetime.
Treating sizeof(pointer) as the number of bytes in the pointed-to array.
Checking for signed overflow after the overflowing expression has already been evaluated. Check the operands before arithmetic.

selfTest.q: Does two's-complement representation guarantee signed wraparound in C++20?
selfTest.a: No. Representation and arithmetic semantics are separate; signed arithmetic overflow remains undefined.

selfTest.q: Can a one-past pointer be used as an end sentinel? Can it be read through?
selfTest.a: It can be compared with pointers into that array. It cannot be dereferenced.

selfTest.q: A function returns a span over a local array. Is its length enough to make it safe?
selfTest.a: No. The local array dies on return, so the span dangles even though it retains the old extent.

selfTest.q: Why does -1 < 1u evaluate to false?
selfTest.a: The int operand converts to unsigned int under the usual arithmetic conversions. -1 becomes the maximum unsigned int value.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: pass native buffers with explicit extents and test empty input, last valid index, invalid index and integer conversion boundaries.
units.stopWhen: Your span operation and checked accessor pass the boundary tests, and you can explain the conversions and lifetime of every pointer or reference they use.

fit.note: The pool covers representation, conversions, pointer bounds and C++20 spans; mini-project buffer tests supply implementation practice.

units.title: Struct layout, alignment, strides and locality
outcomes: Compute field offsets, padding and array strides for a measured native layout.
Derive a byte offset from a base address, index, stride and field offset.
Compare AoS and SoA for a controlled access pattern without assuming either layout must be faster.
units.why: A dtype or stride mismatch changes which bytes native code reads. The same layout choices also decide how much useful data each memory access brings into the computation.

next.note: Validate dtype, shape and byte strides at the extension boundary.
Carry layout reasoning into kernel memory access.

study.title: Objects, representation and alignment
study.locator: Object representation and value representation; Size; Alignment, including the S and X examples
study.depth: Skip implicit object creation and polymorphic layout. Use simple standard-layout structs for offset checks.

study.title: Predictable memory access
study.locator: Per.19: Access memory predictably, including the two matrix traversal orders

study.title: AoS and SoA trade-offs
study.locator: Overview; Topics; AOS Form (Array of Structs); SOA Form (Struct of Arrays)
study.depth: Read the layouts, not the Intel-specific array-notation syntax. Stop before AOSOA and the LIBOR example. Treat performance statements as hypotheses for your own access pattern.

focus: sizeof includes padding. Alignment constrains legal object addresses, and trailing padding keeps successive array elements suitably aligned.
For a standard-layout record array, a field's byte offset is index * sizeof(record) + offsetof(record, field). For a strided view, use the supplied byte strides instead.
AoS groups fields of one record; SoA groups one field across records. Field-wise scans and whole-record access can favor different layouts.
Keep allocation, initialization and layout conversion outside a kernel-only timing. Preserve results so the compiler cannot discard the work, and do not infer cache misses from wall time alone.
units.reproduce: On Linux x86-64 with g++ 15.2, -std=c++20 -O0, define struct Row { char tag; std::int32_t count; char flag; }; print offsetof for all fields, sizeof and alignof. The observed values are offsets 0, 4, 8, size 12 and alignment 4. Thus rows[2].flag is at byte offset 2 * 12 + 8 = 32 from a three-element array's base. These are observations for that toolchain, not universal layout constants. Then compare summing x in vector<Point> where Point has uint64_t x,y,z against a separate vector<uint64_t> x: initialize both with x[i] = i % 100, use 1,048,576 records, g++ 15.2 -std=c++20 -O2, one warmup and seven timed scans per layout in alternating order, and consume each checksum. On the 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K, record all timings and their medians, with sizeof(Point) and allocated bytes. Python is not involved. Both checksums must be 51,903,600; no speed ranking is promised.
traps: Summing member sizes misses internal and trailing padding. Packing a struct is not a free optimization and can create unaligned accesses.
Assuming an array of pointers stores the pointed-to objects contiguously.
Declaring SoA faster from one timing, or comparing different data, access patterns or conversion costs.

selfTest.q: Why can sizeof(Row) exceed the sum of its members' sizes?
selfTest.a: Padding aligns members and successive array elements. The exact amount depends on the implementation and ABI.

selfTest.q: A view has byte strides (40, 8). What is the offset of element [2,3]?
selfTest.a: 2 * 40 + 3 * 8 = 104 bytes from that view's base, assuming the indices are valid.

selfTest.q: Why might SoA help a scan that reads only x, but not a workload consuming every field of scattered records?
selfTest.a: SoA puts successive x values together. Scattered whole-record access instead benefits from keeping each record's fields close, as AoS does. Measure the actual workload.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: document field offsets and strides, then preserve a controlled AoS/SoA comparison with equal checksums and a reproducible measurement setup.
units.stopWhen: Your offset predictions match the measured layout, both scan checksums match, and your seven-repeat report separates measured timings from untested cache explanations.

fit.note: The pool covers alignment and contiguous traversal but lacks a located AoS/SoA comparison; Intel adds the layout trade-offs without requiring its older compiler syntax.

units.title: Storage duration, RAII, smart pointers and move semantics
outcomes: Distinguish storage duration from the lifetime and ownership of an object in that storage.
Predict destruction and resource release through normal returns and caught exceptions.
Implement an owning buffer with independent-copy, ownership-transfer and checked-access tests.
units.why: A buffer can be correctly indexed and still be dead. RAII makes cleanup follow ownership, including failure paths that are easy to miss with manual deletion.

next.note: Use tool evidence to find lifetime failures.
Decide whether Python borrows, copies or owns returned storage.

study.title: Stack vs Heap
study.locator: The Stack: Automatic and LIFO; The Heap: Dynamic and Manual; When to Use the Stack vs the Heap
study.depth: Skip address-region diagrams and Performance Differences. Automatic and dynamic storage duration are language concepts, not guarantees about placement or allocation speed.

study.title: RAII Pattern
study.locator: The Core Idea through Hand-Rolled Cleanup vs RAII Under Exceptions; A Note on the Rule of Three; Almost Always RAII

study.title: Exclusive ownership
study.locator: Constructing a unique_ptr; Move-Only Semantics; The Common Operations; Arrays with unique_ptr<T[]>

study.title: Shared ownership and observers
study.locator: When Shared Ownership Actually Makes Sense; The Control Block; Thread Safety, Precisely; What This Chapter Does Not Cover

study.title: Copy and move contracts
study.locator: The Move Constructor Signature through When the Compiler Generates a Move Constructor; A Complete Example: Cart with Move and Copy
study.depth: Skip the introductory claim that return-by-value necessarily copies and Exercise 7's unconditional noexcept rule. Copy elision can remove transfers, and vector can move a noncopyable element even if its move may throw.

study.title: RAII and special members
study.locator: R.1: Manage resources automatically using resource handles and RAII; C.20: If you can avoid defining default operations, do; C.21: If you define or delete any copy, move, or destructor function, define or delete them all

focus: An automatic smart-pointer handle can own a dynamically allocated object. The handle and the allocation have separate lifetimes.

Scope exit and exception unwinding destroy fully constructed automatic objects in reverse construction order. A constructor that throws does not run that object's destructor, but already constructed members and bases are unwound.
Prefer vector and the Rule of Zero for ordinary buffers. If you manage a raw resource, state copy and move contracts for constructors and assignment, and leave the moved-from object safe to destroy.
unique_ptr expresses exclusive ownership. shared_ptr shares ownership, not synchronization of the pointee; weak_ptr observes without forming a strong ownership cycle.
units.reproduce: With g++ 15.2 -std=c++20 -O0 -g, construct two local logging guards A then B inside a try block and throw std::runtime_error to an outer catch. Print only names from destructors and 'catch' from the handler: the sequence is B A catch. Separately move make_unique<int>(7) into a second unique_ptr and assert the first is null and the second holds 7. Implement a vector-backed Buffer with a deep-copy contract, a custom move that resets the source to an empty state, and access that throws std::out_of_range for i >= size(). Check copy independence, move construction, move assignment, self-assignment, empty access and a caught exception after allocation. Keep the checks active in optimized builds; do not rely only on assert when NDEBUG is set.
traps: std::move is a cast that enables move overloads. It does not itself transfer resources; moving from a const object can select a copy.
A shared_ptr reference count does not collect strong cycles or protect mutable data from concurrent access.
RAII is not a promise of cleanup after process termination, std::abort or every uncaught exception. Test ordinary scope exit and caught unwinding.

selfTest.q: A constructor acquires two resources but the second acquisition throws. How should the first be protected?
selfTest.a: Place it in an already constructed RAII member or local guard. That guard is destroyed during unwinding even though the enclosing object's destructor does not run.

selfTest.q: Does copying a raw owning pointer produce an independent buffer?
selfTest.a: No. It copies the address. Either duplicate the storage explicitly, prohibit copying, or use a value-owning member such as vector.

selfTest.q: After moving a unique_ptr into another, which one owns the object?
selfTest.a: The destination owns it; the source is null. This specific guarantee is stronger than assuming all moved-from types are empty.

selfTest.q: Must a return-by-value function always call a copy or move constructor?
selfTest.a: No. Copy elision can avoid both. C++17 guarantees elision for certain prvalue cases; named return value optimization is permitted but not generally mandatory.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: implement and test the owning buffer's copy, move, checked access and exception-cleanup contracts.
units.stopWhen: You predict the guard destruction trace and your buffer tests demonstrate independent copies, an explicitly empty moved-from state and cleanup through a caught exception.

fit.note: Located AlgoMaster ownership and copy/move examples plus Core Guidelines reach the target; the mini-project supplies the tested buffer, with source overstatements explicitly excluded.

units.title: Templates, containers and iterator invalidation
outcomes: Read a function or class template and identify its type arguments and required operations.
Explain container choice using contiguity, access complexity and iterator stability.
Determine which handles survive a vector mutation without dereferencing invalid ones.
units.why: Native APIs commonly expose templates and STL types. Reading their contracts is enough to make bounded changes without learning advanced metaprogramming.

next.note: Recognize invalidated-handle bugs before investigating a crash.
Choose containers from the operations an algorithm requires.

study.title: Function Templates
study.locator: Anatomy of a Function Template; Template Argument Deduction; Explicit Template Arguments; Implicit vs Explicit Instantiation
study.depth: Stop at reading instantiation syntax. Distinct instantiations are not a guarantee of distinct emitted machine-code bodies.

study.title: Class Templates
study.locator: Declaring a Class Template; Multiple Type Parameters; Member Functions: In-Class vs Out-of-Class; Member Type Aliases; Nested Types and the typename Keyword
study.depth: Skip member templates, friend templates and metaprogramming.

study.title: std::vector
study.locator: Memory Layout: Contiguous Storage; Size vs Capacity; Removing Elements; Accessing Elements; reserve, shrink_to_fit, resize; Iterator Invalidation; Complexity Summary

study.title: Iterators
study.locator: The Generalised Pointer through const_iterator and Read-Only Access; Iterator Invalidation
study.depth: Skip reverse, insert and stream adapters for this pass.

study.title: Container contracts
study.locator: Sequence containers; Associative containers; Unordered associative containers; Iterator invalidation table

study.title: Vector invalidation
study.locator: Iterator invalidation table, particularly reserve, push_back, insert and erase

focus: A template describes compile-time generic code. Identify the operations its body needs from T, and read the first diagnostic referring to your instantiation before the library backtrace.

vector<T> is contiguous for ordinary T, but vector<bool> is a special case. list provides different stability guarantees; unordered containers can invalidate iterators on rehash while preserving references to elements.
reserve changes capacity, not size. Existing elements remain valid after reserve only when no reallocation occurs.
Without reallocation, push_back still invalidates the old end iterator; erase invalidates handles at and after the erased position. Use the iterator returned by erase to continue traversal.
units.reproduce: With g++ 15.2 -std=c++20 -O0 -g, write template<class T> T twice(T x) { return x + x; }. Check twice(3) == 6 and twice(2.5) == 5.0, and explain why a type without a suitable + cannot instantiate the body. For vector<int>{1,2,3}, erase begin()+1 and check the resulting values {1,3} and that the returned iterator points to 3. Predict the invalidated handles before running. Force reallocation using reserve(capacity()+1), then reacquire all handles without comparing or dereferencing the old ones.
traps: An iterator is not necessarily a pointer or random-access. Algorithms impose iterator-category requirements.
Capacity is allocated space, not a range of constructed elements that operator[] may access.
A sanitizer's silence does not make an invalidated iterator valid. Its address may still lie in allocated memory.

selfTest.q: A vector has spare capacity. Does push_back preserve every iterator?
selfTest.a: No. Existing element iterators survive without reallocation, but the old past-the-end iterator is invalidated.

selfTest.q: After reserve(100) on an empty vector, can you write v[0]?
selfTest.a: No. Its size is still zero. Use resize or insert an element first.

selfTest.q: Why can a template definition in a .cpp file produce a link failure for a caller in another translation unit?
selfTest.a: The caller may need the definition to instantiate its argument types. Put the definition where it is visible or supply the needed explicit instantiation in a linked translation unit.

selfTest.q: Why use it = v.erase(it) rather than ++it after erasure?
selfTest.a: The erased iterator is invalid. erase returns a valid iterator to the following element, or the new end.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: review generic buffer code and test container mutations while reacquiring handles according to the invalidation contract.
units.stopWhen: You explain twice's type requirements and the vector erasure result, and correctly classify handles after reserve, push_back, insert, erase and unordered-container rehash.

fit.note: Located AlgoMaster lessons provide the reading pass; cppreference supplies precise invalidation contracts and the mini-project covers mutation review.

units.title: Undefined behavior, sanitizers and debugger evidence
outcomes: Identify bounds, lifetime, double-free, uninitialized-read and overflow hazards in C++20 code.
Build with warnings, debug symbols, ASan and UBSan, then interpret a report's failing access and lifetime history.
Locate a failure in a debugger, repair its root cause and preserve a regression test.
units.why: Undefined behavior has no promised result, including a crash. Tool evidence helps locate a violated contract without turning one observed output into a language rule.

next.note: Keep diagnostic builds and regression tests repeatable.
Diagnose native failures without relying on Python exceptions to contain them.

study.title: Undefined behavior
study.locator: Explanation; UB and optimization: Signed overflow, Access out of bounds and Uninitialized scalar
study.depth: Use the C++20 rules. Do not mistake displayed assembly for guaranteed behavior; the C++26 erroneous-behavior distinction is outside this unit.

study.title: AddressSanitizer
study.locator: Introduction; Usage and example_UseAfterFree.cc; Symbolizing the Reports; Additional Checks: Stack Use After Return and Memory leak detection; Limitations

study.title: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer
study.locator: Introduction; Usage; Available checks, including signed-integer-overflow and the undefined group; Stack traces and report symbolization
study.depth: Skip runtime suppression, minimal runtime and newer overflow-behavior attributes.

study.title: Debugger backtraces
study.locator: 8.2 Backtraces: bt, -full, frame numbering and optimized-out arguments
study.depth: Skip frame filters and backtrace formatting options.

focus: Bounds and lifetime are separate contracts. A stale pointer may still point inside mapped memory; reading it remains invalid.

ASan reports memory-access violations with allocation and deallocation stacks. UBSan checks selected undefined operations, including signed overflow; the default undefined group is not a check for every possible defect.
Preserve the command, compiler version, input and first report. Repair the invalid lifetime or index calculation rather than suppressing the report.
A debugger gives frames and state, not proof that a program has defined behavior. A clean dynamic-tool run covers only executed paths and enabled checks.
units.reproduce: Run LLVM's example_UseAfterFree.cc with no extra arguments, using clang++ 21.1 -std=c++20 -O1 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer. Preserve the report: the checked run reports 'AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free' and 'READ of size 4', with the allocation, delete[] and subsequent read identified. The unsanitized program has undefined behavior and no particular output is guaranteed. Repair it using initialized owned storage that remains alive until after the read, and rerun with the same flags. In a separate program, add argc to numeric_limits<int>::max(): the same diagnostic build reports 'signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type int' on this Linux x86-64 toolchain. A default recoverable UBSan report need not produce a nonzero exit; use -fno-sanitize-recover=undefined for a failing test target. On a repaired -O0 -g build, run gdb, break main, run and bt to connect the source location to its frame.
traps: ASan and UBSan do not generally detect uninitialized-value use. MemorySanitizer is a separate tool, not part of -fsanitize=address,undefined.
A data race is outside ASan/UBSan's usual checks. ThreadSanitizer requires a separate build and cannot be combined with AddressSanitizer.
A successful exit is not enough: UBSan can recover after reporting a violation, and an unexecuted bad path remains unchecked.

selfTest.q: A use-after-free program prints the expected value. Is the read valid?
selfTest.a: No. Its object lifetime ended. Undefined behavior guarantees no particular output, including apparent success.

selfTest.q: What evidence distinguishes an invalid index from a freed-buffer access?
selfTest.a: The report's access location and region bounds, plus allocation and deallocation history. Use that history to check the bounds and lifetime independently.

selfTest.q: Why can a UBSan-instrumented test exit zero despite a signed-overflow report?
selfTest.a: Many checks recover by default. Configure non-recovery when a violation must fail the test process.

selfTest.q: Does a clean ASan/UBSan run prove there are no uninitialized reads or data races?
selfTest.a: No. These tools do not generally cover those defect classes, nor paths that did not execute.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: preserve a seeded memory defect's first sanitizer report, locate it with debugger evidence, repair the root cause and add a regression test.
units.stopWhen: You explain the failing access from its report, preserve a regression that fails on the seeded defect and passes after repair, and name what the enabled tools still cannot prove.

fit.note: Kept LLVM's reproducible defects and cppreference's C++20 rules; added GDB Backtraces because the pool lacked a verified debugger-command locator.
